title: Clothes shopping, colors, and comparisons
goal: Buying clothes in the right size and color — and comparing two things, which Egyptian does with one word form for everything.
bekal: comparing two things with the أفعل form and the word من
asking to try on, exchange, or change the size

dialogs.title: حوار — قميص أزرق
dialogs.intro: Budi is looking for a shirt for the dinner invitation at Mona's home. He walks into a clothes shop in Maadi.

lines.speaker: البياعة:
lines.id: Hi! Looking for anything in particular?

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: أيوه، عايز قميص. حاجة رسمية شوية.
lines.id: Yes, I want a shirt. Something a bit formal.
lines.literal: yes, want shirt. thing formal a-little.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: I'm not sure exactly. Medium, I think.

lines.speaker: البياعة:
lines.id: Take this one and try it on. The fitting room is over there.
lines.literal: take this and measure-it. the-room there.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: ده ضيق عليا شوية. فيه أكبر؟
lines.id: This is a bit tight on me. Is there a bigger one?
lines.literal: this tight on-me a-little. there-is bigger?

lines.speaker: البياعة:
lines.id: Sure. This is a large. Try it.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: أحسن كتير. بس اللون ده غامق أوي.
lines.baca: ahsan kitiir. bas il-lōn da ghaami’ ’awi.
lines.id: Much better. But this color is too dark.
lines.literal: better much. but the-color this dark very.

lines.speaker: البياعة:
lines.text: فيه نفس الموديل أزرق فاتح. أحلى كمان.
lines.baca: fiih nafs il-modēl azra’ faatih. ahla kamaan.
lines.id: We have the same style in light blue. Even nicer.
lines.literal: there-is same the-model blue light. sweeter also.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.text: أيوه، ده أحلى من الأول. بكام؟
lines.id: Yes, this one's nicer than the first. How much?
lines.literal: yes, this sweeter than the-first. for-how-much?

lines.speaker: البياعة:
lines.text: أربعمية وخمسين. قطن مية في المية.
lines.id: Four hundred fifty. A hundred percent cotton.
lines.literal: four-hundred and-fifty. cotton hundred in the-hundred.

lines.speaker: البياعة:
lines.baca: khalliiha arba‘miyya, wi da aakhir si‘r.
lines.id: Let's say four hundred, and that's my final price.
lines.literal: let-it four-hundred, and this last price.

lines.speaker: بودي:
lines.id: Okay. If it doesn't work out, can I exchange it?

lines.speaker: البياعة:
lines.id: Of course, within a week, with the receipt. Enjoy it!

notes: **Arabic has just one comparison form for everything**: the أفعل pattern. The word كبير becomes أكبر, the word حلو becomes أحلى, and the word كويس becomes أحسن. It means both "-er" and "-est", depending on word order, and it **doesn't change** for masculine or feminine.

**The word for "than" in Egyptian is من.** أحلى من الأول (nicer than the first one), أكبر مني (bigger than me). It's exactly the Fusha pattern, and also exactly the pattern of Hebrew and Aramaic — a hallmark of the Semitic languages.
**The word نفس means "same" when it stands before a noun.** نفس الموديل (the same style), نفس الحاجة (the same thing), في نفس الوقت (at the same time). On its own, نفس means "soul" or "self".
**The words غامق and فاتح describe the depth of a color**, not how bright a room is: أزرق غامق (dark blue), أزرق فاتح (light blue). For a dark room, the word is ضلمة *ḍalma*.
**People say مبروك when someone buys something**, not just for weddings and graduations. New shoes, a new phone, a new haircut — all deserve a مبروك. The reply is الله يبارك فيك.
**The phrase لو مانفعش uses the verb نفع, "to be of use, to work".** It's very common in the negative: مش حاينفع (it won't work), ماينفعش كده (you can't do that). As an adjective: نافع (useful).

grammars.title: More, and most
body: One word form handles both. The only difference is where it stands in the sentence.
after: The word-order rule: **after** a noun it means "more" — بيت أكبر (a bigger house). **Before** a noun it means "most" — أكبر بيت (the biggest house). One form, two meanings, told apart by order.

Row three is irregular and must be memorized: the comparative of كويس isn't أكوس but **أحسن** — just like English good → better. It's one of the most used words in Egyptian, so it'll stick on its own soon enough.
To say two things are equal, use زي *zayy*: ده زي ده (this is like this), أنا زيك (I'm just like you). The word زي also means "like" in comparisons.

grammars.title: Colors, and their unusual forms
body: Basic colors in Arabic have their own pattern that doesn't follow ordinary adjectives: masculine uses أفعل, feminine uses فعلا.
after: Notice that **the first six colors** use the special pattern, while the rest are ordinary adjectives formed from nouns: بني from بن (coffee beans), برتقاني from برتقان (oranges), رمادي from رماد (ash).
The masculine form of a color happens to look exactly like a comparative: أحمر and أكبر. But they're not related at all, and colors have no comparative form.

blocks.text: Clothing sizes in Egypt use localized English terms: سمول *smōl*, ميديم *midyum*, لارج *laarg*, إكس لارج. Shoe sizes use European numbers, and the question is مقاس رجلك كام؟

blocks.title: The word جزمة and shoe etiquette
items: The word جزمة comes from Turkish *çizme*, and it means any kind of shoe — not just boots.
In Egypt, shoes are considered dirty in a fairly literal sense. Putting shoes on a table, or pointing the sole of your shoe at someone while crossing your legs, is seen as rude.
Taking off your shoes in someone's home isn't always expected in urban Egypt — wait for your host's cue. If in doubt, ask: أخلع الجزمة؟

blocks.text: These sentences cover almost an entire visit to a clothes shop, from walking in to walking out with a receipt.

The phrase بس بتفرج is the key to peace in an Egyptian market. It tells the seller you're not ready to buy yet, and it's almost always answered with اتفضل، براحتك ("go ahead, take your time"). Without it, you'll be followed around with offers.
